questions.question: What is microservices architecture?

options.text: A single large application deployed as one unit
An architecture where applications are composed of small, independent services that communicate over networks
A database design pattern for horizontal scaling
A frontend framework for building user interfaces

questions.explanation: Microservices decompose applications into small, independently deployable services. Each service owns its data, has a specific business capability, and communicates via APIs. Netflix pioneered this at scale with 700+ microservices; Amazon's retail site comprises thousands. This enables team autonomy, independent scaling, and technology diversity—but adds significant operational complexity.

questions.question: Which are benefits of microservices? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Independent deployment of services
Technology diversity—different services can use different tech stacks
Simpler architecture than monoliths
Easier scaling of individual components

questions.explanation: Microservices benefits: independent deployment (change one service without affecting others—Amazon deploys thousands of times daily), tech diversity (use Python for ML, Go for performance-critical services), targeted scaling (scale only the bottleneck). NOT simpler—distributed systems add significant complexity in debugging, data consistency, and operations. The complexity is the price of flexibility.

questions.question: What is a key challenge of microservices?

options.text: Architecture is too simple to handle complex domains
Distributed system complexity: network failures, data consistency, debugging
Cannot scale beyond a single server
Requires all services to use the same programming language

questions.explanation: Microservices introduce distributed systems challenges: networks are unreliable (the fallacies of distributed computing), maintaining data consistency across services requires patterns like Saga, debugging spans multiple services requiring distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin), and operational complexity increases dramatically. Google's SRE book documents these challenges extensively.

questions.question: How should microservices handle data?

options.text: Share a single database for consistency
Each service owns its data; no direct database sharing
Use only in-memory storage for performance
Store all data in a central file system

questions.explanation: Database per service: each microservice owns its data, accessed only through its API. No shared databases—this would couple services and defeat the purpose. Enables independent schema changes, technology choices (SQL vs NoSQL per service), and scaling. Shopify migrated from shared database to service-owned data to enable team autonomy. The tradeoff: cross-service queries become harder.

questions.question: What is the recommended size for a microservice?

options.text: Exactly 100 lines of code or less
Small enough for one team to own; large enough to provide meaningful business capability
As small as technically possible
One function per service (nanoservices)

questions.explanation: Size isn't about code lines—it's about ownership and capability. A service should be owned by one team (Amazon's 'two-pizza team' rule) and represent a cohesive business capability (bounded context in DDD terms). Too small creates overhead and chattiness; too large becomes a mini-monolith. Spotify's squads own services that map to user-facing features.

questions.question: When should you NOT use microservices?

options.text: When you have a small team and simple domain
When you need high scalability for specific components
When you have multiple autonomous teams
When services have clear bounded contexts

questions.explanation: Microservices add significant overhead. Small teams with simple domains are better served by monoliths—less complexity, faster development, easier debugging. Martin Fowler calls this 'Monolith First.' Microservices shine with multiple teams needing autonomy, complex domains with clear boundaries, and specific scaling needs. Basecamp runs a successful monolith; not every company needs Netflix's architecture.

questions.question: How do microservices typically communicate? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Synchronous REST/gRPC calls
Asynchronous messaging (events, queues)
Shared memory between processes
Direct database queries to other services' databases

questions.explanation: Microservices communicate via: synchronous calls (REST for simplicity, gRPC for performance) for request-response patterns, and asynchronous messaging (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) for event-driven communication. NOT shared memory (services run in separate processes/containers) or direct DB queries (violates encapsulation and creates tight coupling). Uber uses both: gRPC for real-time and Kafka for analytics.

questions.question: What is 'service mesh' in microservices?

options.text: A network topology diagram showing service dependencies
Infrastructure layer handling service-to-service communication, security, and observability
A NoSQL database optimized for microservices data
A container orchestration and deployment platform

questions.explanation: Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect) is dedicated infrastructure for service communication. It handles load balancing, mTLS encryption, authentication, retries, circuit breaking, and observability—all without application code changes. Lyft created Envoy proxy for this purpose. The mesh offloads cross-cutting concerns from application code to infrastructure, but adds operational complexity.

questions.question: True or False: Microservices eliminate the need for careful API design.

options.text: True - services are independent so APIs don't matter
False - API design becomes even more critical

questions.explanation: API design is MORE critical in microservices. APIs are contracts between services—breaking changes affect all dependent services. You need versioning strategies, backward compatibility, clear documentation, and contract testing. Stripe's API is famous for maintaining backward compatibility for years. Poor API design in microservices creates the 'distributed monolith' anti-pattern.

questions.question: What is the 'distributed monolith' anti-pattern?

options.text: A well-designed microservices system with clear boundaries
Microservices that are tightly coupled, requiring coordinated deployments
A single-server application handling all requests
A database sharding pattern for horizontal scaling

questions.explanation: Distributed monolith: services are technically separate but tightly coupled—changes require coordinated deployments, shared databases exist, synchronous call chains create dependencies. You get the worst of both worlds: distributed complexity without independence benefits. This often happens when teams split a monolith by technical layer (UI, business logic, data) instead of by business capability.

questions.question: How should microservices handle failures in dependent services?

options.text: Crash immediately to alert operators
Implement resilience patterns: circuit breakers, retries, fallbacks, timeouts
Ignore failures and return empty responses
Wait indefinitely for the service to recover

questions.explanation: Microservices must handle failures gracefully—failures are normal in distributed systems. Use circuit breakers (Netflix Hystrix pattern—stop calling failing services), retries with exponential backoff, fallbacks (return cached data or degraded functionality), and timeouts (don't wait forever). Amazon's retail site degrades gracefully: if recommendations fail, the page still loads with products.

questions.question: What organizational structure supports microservices best?

options.text: Centralized team owning all services
Cross-functional teams owning services end-to-end (Conway's Law)
Separate teams for frontend, backend, and database
One developer assigned per service

questions.explanation: Conway's Law: system design mirrors organization structure. Cross-functional teams (developers, ops, QA) owning services end-to-end work best—they can deploy independently without coordination. Amazon's 'two-pizza teams' and Spotify's 'squads' follow this model. Siloed teams (frontend/backend/DB) create coordination overhead and coupling, defeating microservices benefits.
